claims.text: Coating tungsten particles with few-layer graphene before consolidation will create an ultrathin graphene interlayer at tungsten–copper interfaces.
A similarly high-thermal-conductivity 2D material could substitute for few-layer graphene in this intervention.
The graphene interlayer will lower thermal resistance at tungsten–copper interfaces.
Graphene has extremely high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Graphene's intrinsic thermal conductivity will provide efficient heat transport across tungsten–copper interfaces.
The graphene interlayer will have sufficiently robust bonding to the composite constituents to preserve mechanical load transfer.
The ultrathin profile of the graphene interlayer will help preserve mechanical load transfer.
The graphene interlayer will remain stable under irradiation representative of fusion-reactor service.
The graphene-coated W–Cu composite will have higher overall thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical uncoated W–Cu composite.
The graphene-coated composite will retain mechanical durability or toughness relative to the uncoated W–Cu baseline.
The graphene-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to the uncoated W–Cu baseline.
Fusion-reactor applications expose materials to severe temperature, stress, heat flux, particle flux, and radiation conditions.
High-temperature cyclic thermal loading and simulated irradiation are representative application conditions for W–Cu fusion-reactor joints.
Degradation of the graphene layer under extreme irradiation would reduce the thermal benefit.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity increase will depend on graphene-coating uniformity and quality.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity increase will depend on the graphene coating's behavior under prolonged irradiation.
